title: Torrontés
description: Argentina's own white grape: intensely floral, grown at some of the world's highest vineyards.
L: Torrontés gives intensely aromatic whites with rose, jasmine, orange blossom, peach, lemon and lychee. Most are dry, with medium acidity and medium to high alcohol, and sometimes a slightly bitter finish. Its perfume makes it seem sweet, but it's usually dry.

There are three Torrontés: Riojano, the finest and most planted, Sanjuanino and Mendocino. DNA shows Torrontés Riojano is a cross of Muscat of Alexandria and Criolla Chica, also called Listán Prieto or País, brought by Spanish colonists. That explains its Muscat-like perfume. It's Argentina's own grape, born there.

Look for pale lemon colour and an explosive floral nose of rose and orange blossom, then a dry palate with medium acidity and warm alcohol. A slight bitterness at the end is typical. Compared with Muscat, it's often drier and spicier; compared with Gewürztraminer, fresher.

Explain how altitude shapes its style

Torrontés Riojano grows best in the Calchaquí Valleys of Salta, in north-west Argentina, around Cafayate, at 1,700 to over 3,000 m, among the highest vineyards in the world. It's also grown in La Rioja, the province that gave it its name, and in Mendoza and San Juan.

At such altitude, days are hot and sunny, with intense ultraviolet light, while nights are cold. Torrontés ripens fully, developing its aromas, but keeps acidity. The UV thickens skins, adding aroma compounds. Without altitude, in hot lowlands, Torrontés can be flabby, bitter and too alcoholic.
Sun by day, cold at night
Torrontés is at its best high in the north.

Winemakers keep Torrontés fresh: cool fermentation in steel, no oak, early bottling. Some pick earlier to reduce alcohol and bitterness. A few producers make oaked, late harvest or sparkling versions, but the fresh, dry style dominates.
Cold nights keep acidity while sun ripens aromas
Altitude gives a large day and night swing, balancing ripeness and freshness.
Torrontés thrives in Salta's high valleys, around Cafayate
Altitude keeps acidity while sun ripens aromas
Know how long to keep it

Torrontés suits aromatic, lightly spiced food: Thai, Indian, Vietnamese dishes, ceviche, and Argentine empanadas from Salta, filled with spiced beef. Its floral perfume and freshness suit coriander, ginger and lemongrass. Avoid heavy, rich sauces.
Serve at 7 to 10 degrees. Torrontés is best young, within one to two years, while its aromas are fresh. With age, it can turn bitter and lose its perfume.
